body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Accuracy of the 30-second sit-to-stand test for a low anaerobic threshold before major abdominal surgery","authors":"Okonkwo-Brandvold T, Laurent-Mensah P, Ishikawa-Reid A","year":2021,"venue":"Perioperative Medicine and Fitness","doi":"10.5555/pmf.2021.0144","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 212 consecutive patients awaiting major abdominal surgery, the 30-second sit-to-stand test was compared with cardiopulmonary exercise testing. A count of 10 or fewer identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 78 percent and specificity 69 percent. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.77. Testers knew the exercise test results in a third of patients, and 14 patients who could not complete exercise testing were excluded. The cut-off was chosen in the same data, which may overstate accuracy in new patients."},{"title":"Gait speed and anaerobic threshold in older surgical patients: a small comparison","authors":"Varga-Achterberg L, Oduya-Castellanos M","year":null,"venue":"Anaesthesia research meeting abstract book","providerType":"conference-abstract","abstract":"In 64 patients aged 65 or older scheduled for major surgery, gait speed over four metres was compared with the anaerobic threshold from exercise testing. Gait speed below 1.0 m/s identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 71 percent and specificity 62 percent. The abstract does not state the year of the meeting, the recruitment period, how patients were selected or whether testers were blinded. The abstract gives no information about losses to follow-up or missing exercise tests."},{"title":"Field tests of functional capacity against cardiopulmonary exercise testing before major surgery: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy","authors":"Rasmussen-Obi H, Petrakis-Nwosu D, Svensson-Achebe K, Tanaka-Holt R","year":2019,"venue":"Perioperative Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/per.2019.0228","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 15 studies comparing simple field tests (sit-to-stand, gait speed, stair climbing, incremental shuttle walk) with the anaerobic threshold from exercise testing before major surgery. Sensitivity for a low anaerobic threshold ranged from 62 to 81 percent and specificity from 55 to 78 percent. Most studies were at high risk of bias in patient selection and blinding, and no study validated a cut-off in a separate sample. Patients unable to complete exercise testing were usually excluded. No field test was accurate enough to replace exercise testing for individual risk assessment."},{"title":"Combining sit-to-stand and gait speed to triage patients for prehabilitation: a service report","authors":"Surgical prehabilitation service, Kestrelmoor General Hospital","year":null,"venue":"Hospital service improvement bulletin","providerType":"report","abstract":"A single hospital combined the 30-second sit-to-stand test and gait speed to decide which patients were offered supervised prehabilitation. The service reports that most patients it judged high risk were identified by the combination, but exercise testing was done only in patients with abnormal bedside results, so accuracy cannot be calculated. Uptake of prehabilitation rose after the triage change. The report gives no date, no numbers for the patients tested and no description of how the combination rule was chosen."},{"title":"Prehabilitation places, waiting times and postoperative complications at a regional surgical centre","authors":"Mbeki-Lindqvist S, Ferreira-Dube J","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Surgical Pathways","doi":"10.5555/jsp.2023.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 540 patients undergoing major abdominal surgery at one centre, those who completed at least four weeks of supervised prehabilitation had fewer postoperative complications than those who did not, but patients who completed the program were younger and fitter. Of patients prioritised for a place by exercise testing, 46 percent started prehabilitation too late to complete four weeks before surgery because they waited for the test. The authors argue that faster triage matters as much as the choice of triage test."},{"title":"Patients unable to complete cardiopulmonary exercise testing before major surgery: frequency and outcomes","authors":"Nakamura-Fischer O, Brennan-Oyelaran B","year":2017,"venue":"Perioperative Medicine and Fitness","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Of 1,120 patients referred for exercise testing before major surgery, 9 percent could not complete a test, most often because of joint pain, frailty or breathlessness at low workloads. These patients had the highest rate of postoperative complications in the cohort. Accuracy studies that excluded them would overstate the specificity of any bedside test, because the patients most likely to fail both tests are removed. The authors recommend a pre-specified rule that classifies inability to complete testing as low functional capacity."},{"title":"Sample size for diagnostic accuracy studies when the target condition prevalence is uncertain: a practical guide","authors":"Halvorsen-Adeyemi E, Quist-Morales R, Sato-Kowalczyk N","year":2025,"venue":"Diagnostic Research Methods","doi":"10.5555/drm.2025.0012","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We give worked examples for planning accuracy studies. Estimating a sensitivity of 80 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of plus or minus 10 percentage points needs about 62 patients with the target condition; if the prevalence is 40 percent, about 155 patients must be recruited. We recommend inflating the total for patients without a usable reference result, pre-specifying cut-offs from earlier studies, and reporting accuracy for a second cut-off only as exploratory. Choosing a cut-off in the same data inflates both sensitivity and specificity."}]}
